subject: Social Science
title: The Economy is Everywhere: How People Produce and Trade
hook: How do villages and cities produce goods? How does food reach your plate? How does money move?

characters.name: Ananya
characters.role: A curious 12-year-old from a town in Maharashtra

characters.name: Farmer Bhagwan
characters.role: Ananya's uncle who grows sugarcane and sells it to a factory

characters.name: Mr. Patel
characters.role: A shop owner who sells goods from many local and distant producers

slides.title: Economic Activities Around Us
slides.storyContext: Ananya buys lunch at school: rice (from Punjab), curry (with vegetables from a farm near her town), chapati (wheat from Madhya Pradesh), salt (from Gujarat). In an hour, she's consumed products from 5 different regions, made by hundreds of people, bought and sold by traders. She doesn't realize it, but she's witnessing 'the economy' in action.

image.alt: Economic Activities Around Us — Economic Activities Around Us

slides.title: From Field to Table
slides.storyContext: Farmer Bhagwan grows sugarcane on his 5-acre farm. He sells it to a sugar factory 30 km away. The factory processes it into sugar and sells it to wholesalers in the city. The wholesalers sell to shop owners like Mr. Patel. Mr. Patel sells sugar to families like Ananya's. Along the way: the farmer earned income, the factory created jobs, traders made profit, shopkeeper provided service. The 'economy' is this entire chain of production and trade.

slides.title: What is an Economy? Production, Distribution, and Consumption
slides.storyContext: An economy is how a society organizes to produce what people need, distribute it fairly, and consume it without waste.

points.label: Production
points.text: Creating goods (food, clothes, tools) and services (teaching, healing, transportation). Farmers produce food; factories produce goods; teachers provide services.

points.label: Distribution
points.text: Moving goods from producers to consumers. Traders, transporters, shopkeepers, and wholesalers handle distribution. They earn profit.

points.label: Consumption
points.text: People using goods and services. A family consumes food, clothes, and healthcare. A business consumes raw materials.

points.label: Flow of money
points.text: Money moves in reverse: consumers pay shopkeepers, who pay wholesalers, who pay factories, who pay farmers. This circular flow sustains the economy.

example.problem: Trace the economy for a cotton shirt: (1) Who produces it? (2) How does it reach the shop? (3) How do different people earn?
example.solution: (1) Farmer grows cotton → mill spins thread → factory stitches shirt. (2) Factory sells to wholesaler → wholesaler to retailer → retailer to customer. (3) Farmer earns from cotton, mill worker earns wage, factory owner earns profit, retailer earns markup, transporter earns fee. Everyone in the chain benefits.

slides.inSimpleWords: An economy is the system of producing, distributing, and consuming goods. Money moves through this system, supporting everyone involved.

slides.title: Agricultural Economy: Farming and Food Production
slides.storyContext: Ananya's region is agricultural. Most people farm or work in farm-related jobs: making tools, storing grains, selling produce, processing food.

points.label: Subsistence farming
points.text: A farmer grows food mainly for his own family's consumption. No surplus to sell. Common in poorer regions.

points.label: Commercial farming
points.text: A farmer grows crops specifically for sale (sugarcane, cotton, wheat, spices). Tries to maximize yield and profit.

points.label: Cropping patterns in India
points.text: Rice and wheat (staples) in North, spices in South, cotton in Gujarat/Andhra, sugarcane in Maharashtra/Uttar Pradesh, tea in Assam/Himachal.

points.label: Agricultural support
points.text: Government helps through subsidies (cheaper seeds/fertilizer), irrigation, crop insurance, and minimum support prices (MSP).

example.problem: Farmer Bhagwan grew sugarcane but faced two problems: (1) unseasonal rain damaged 20% of the crop, (2) a factory paid less than last year. How does the government help?
example.solution: (1) Crop insurance compensates for weather damage. (2) Minimum Support Price (MSP) guarantees a floor price—if the market price drops below MSP, the government buys at MSP. This gives farmers security.

slides.inSimpleWords: Farming is a major economic activity in India. Farmers produce food and cash crops. The government helps farmers through subsidies and price support.

image.alt: Agricultural Economy: Farming and Food Production — Economic Activities Around Us

slides.title: Industrial Economy: Manufacturing and Factories
slides.storyContext: Ananya visits a sugar factory near her town. She sees: sugarcane entering, machines processing, sugar bags being packaged and loaded onto trucks. The factory employs 200 workers, runs 24/7, and produces 500 tons of sugar daily.

points.label: What are industries?
points.text: Businesses that use machines and labor to transform raw materials into finished products. Cotton → fabric → clothes. Sugarcane → sugar.

points.label: Types of industries
points.text: Primary (extractive): mining, forestry. Secondary (manufacturing): textile mills, sugar factories, steel plants. Tertiary (services): transport, shops, schools.

points.label: Cottage industries
points.text: Small-scale, home-based production (pottery, weaving, handicrafts). Employ 1-5 people. Important for rural income.

points.label: Factory jobs and working conditions
points.text: Factories provide employment but workers often face low wages, long hours, and unsafe conditions. Labor laws protect workers' rights.

example.problem: A textile factory produces 1000 shirts daily. Its output over a year is 365,000 shirts. This creates jobs for 100 workers, income for cotton farmers, and profit for the owner. But a worker earns only 10,000/month. Is this fair?
example.solution: The worker should earn at least the minimum wage (varies by state, typically 8,000-12,000/month). If the factory profits are high, workers should share in the gains. Worker unions and labor laws push for fair wages.

slides.inSimpleWords: Factories use machines and workers to make goods from raw materials. They create jobs and income but must treat workers fairly.

slides.title: Service Economy: Doctors, Teachers, Shops, Transportation
slides.storyContext: Services are invisible but essential. Ananya's school teacher (education), the doctor at the clinic (health), the rickshaw driver (transport), and shop owners (retail) all provide services.

points.label: What are services?
points.text: Intangible work that helps or serves people: teaching, healthcare, transportation, entertainment, banking, government. Services don't produce physical goods.

points.label: Growing importance
points.text: In developed economies, services dominate (over 70% of GDP). In India, it's 55% and growing as people get richer.

points.label: Informal services
points.text: Street vendors, auto-rickshaw drivers, domestic workers, small repair shops—these provide crucial services but are unorganized and underpaid.

points.label: Formal services
points.text: Hospitals, schools, banks, government offices—regulated, with fixed prices/fees and employee protections.

example.problem: Ananya's father uses these services in a month: doctor (500), school (5,000), bus transport (200), restaurant (1,500), barber (100). Total: 7,300 spent on services. Does services cost too much?
example.solution: Services are expensive because they require skilled people's time. A good teacher justifies their fee; a good doctor, their consultation fee. But many services (schools, buses) are subsidized by government to keep them affordable. The market price alone would exclude the poor.

slides.inSimpleWords: Services like teaching, healthcare, and transportation don't make physical goods but are crucial to society. They're a growing part of the economy.

slides.title: Trade and Markets: How Goods Flow Between Regions
slides.storyContext: Ananya's lunch has ingredients from 5 states. Sugar from Maharashtra reaches her town through traders. A trader buys in bulk from the factory, sells to wholesalers, who sell to retailers. Each earns a markup.

points.label: Why trade?
points.text: Different regions produce different goods based on climate, soil, and resources. Trade lets people access goods from everywhere. Coffee grows in South, rice in North. Trade connects them.

points.label: Local markets
points.text: Villages and towns have weekly markets where farmers sell produce and artisans sell goods. Face-to-face trading.

points.label: Regional and national trade
points.text: Wholesale markets (mandis) aggregate goods. Traders, middlemen, and transporters move goods across states. Cities have large retail markets.

points.label: Markup and profit
points.text: Each intermediary (wholesaler, transporter, retailer) adds a markup. This is how they earn. But too many middlemen inflate prices.

example.problem: Sugarcane costs the farmer 400 per quintal. The factory pays 500 (profit: 100). The wholesaler marks up to 600 (100 profit). The retailer to 700 (100 profit). The final price to consumers is 700. Is this fair?
example.solution: It depends on services rendered. The factory processes (labor, machines). The wholesaler stores and transports (cost and risk). The retailer has a shop and serves customers. Each markup reflects their service. But if there are too many middlemen with no value-add, the final price becomes high and farmers get squeezed. The government is promoting direct-to-consumer trade (farmers selling directly in markets, cutting middlemen).

slides.inSimpleWords: Trade connects different regions. Goods flow from producers to consumers through traders and markets. Each person in the chain adds value.

image.alt: Trade and Markets: How Goods Flow Between Regions — Economic Activities Around Us

slides.title: Money and Banking: How Transactions Work
slides.storyContext: Farmer Bhagwan sells sugarcane for 50,000 rupees. He deposits this in a bank. Later, he borrows 100,000 at 8% interest to buy fertilizer. The bank takes his deposit money from others and lends it to him. This is how money circulates in the economy.

points.label: Money's role
points.text: Money is a medium of exchange. Without it, people would barter (trade directly). Money makes transactions efficient.

points.label: Banking system
points.text: Banks accept deposits from people, pay interest, and lend to others at higher interest. The difference is their profit.

points.label: Credit and loans
points.text: Farmers borrow for seeds and fertilizer. Businesses borrow to expand. People borrow to build houses. Banks enable economic growth through lending.

points.label: Interest rates and inflation
points.text: High interest rates discourage borrowing. Low rates encourage it. The central bank (RBI in India) sets policy rates to manage the economy.

example.problem: Farmer Bhagwan borrows 100,000 at 8% interest for 1 year. How much must he repay?
example.solution: 100,000 + (100,000 x 8/100) = 100,000 + 8,000 = 108,000. If his sugarcane harvest yields 150,000 profit, he can repay easily. But if the harvest fails (weather, pest), he's in debt. This is why crop insurance exists.

slides.inSimpleWords: Banks accept money from savers and lend it to borrowers at interest. This helps businesses and individuals grow. Money circulates through the economy.

slides.title: Challenge: A Complete Economic Chain
slides.storyContext: Trace the complete economic chain for a piece of clothing—from cotton production to your wardrobe. Identify: (1) All producers/workers involved, (2) All transactions and money flows, (3) All services provided.

example.problem: A cotton shirt costs 500 in a shop. Trace where this money goes. Start with: Farmer grows cotton (earns ?), Mill processes cotton (earns ?), Factory stitches shirt (earns ?), Transporter delivers (earns ?), Retailer sells (earns ?).
example.solution: One breakdown: Farmer 80, Miller 60, Factory 120, Transporter 40, Retailer markup 200 (profit after costs). Total = 500. This shows how a price is built by multiple contributors. Different markups reflect different efforts and risks.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every product involves many workers, businesses, and services. Money distributed among them is how the economy sustains millions of people.

slides.title: The Economy is Everywhere
slides.storyContext: Ananya now sees that every meal, every object, and every service is part of a vast economic web. Farmers, factories, traders, shopkeepers, and service providers all connect.

points.text: An economy produces, distributes, and consumes goods and services.
Agricultural economy: farming is a major sector, supported by government subsidies and MSP.
Industrial economy: factories transform raw materials into finished goods and employ workers.
Service economy: teachers, doctors, transporters, shopkeepers provide essential services.
Trade and markets connect regions. Traders, wholesalers, and retailers facilitate exchange.
Money and banking enable transactions and help businesses and people grow.

slides.inSimpleWords: The economy is everywhere—in food, clothes, schools, hospitals, shops. It works because millions of people produce, trade, and serve each other.

subject: Mathematics
title: Raj's Geometry Adventure
hook: Raj discovers lines and angles hidden in his apartment building.

slides.title: The Discovery
slides.storyContext: Raj looks out his window and sees the edges of buildings. Meera points out that edges are really lines.
slides.inSimpleWords: Lines are straight paths that go on forever.

image.alt: The Discovery — Lines and Angles

slides.title: What is a Line?
slides.storyContext: Meera draws a line on paper with a ruler. She explains that a line has no endpoints and goes on infinitely.

points.label: Definition
points.text: A line is a straight path with no endpoints, extending infinitely in both directions.

slides.inSimpleWords: A line never ends, it keeps going forever both ways.

image.alt: What is a Line? — Lines and Angles

slides.title: Line Segment and Ray
slides.storyContext: Raj sees the edge of his table (line segment) and the beam of sunlight (ray) coming through the window.

points.label: Line Segment
points.text: A line segment has two endpoints. Example: the edge of Raj's desk.

points.label: Ray
points.text: A ray has one starting point and extends infinitely in one direction. Example: sunlight from a window.

slides.inSimpleWords: A segment has two ends, a ray has one starting point.

image.alt: Line Segment and Ray — Lines and Angles

slides.title: What is an Angle?
slides.storyContext: Meera opens a book like a door hinge. She says the opening between the pages is an angle.

points.label: Angle
points.text: An angle is formed when two rays meet at a common point called the vertex.

slides.inSimpleWords: An angle is the space between two rays meeting at a point.

image.alt: What is an Angle? — Lines and Angles

slides.title: Types of Angles
slides.storyContext: Raj measures different angles at home: the door (90°), a clock hand position (45°), and a stretched rope (180°).

example.solution: 35° is acute (less than 90°), 90° is right, 120° is obtuse (between 90° and 180°), 180° is straight.

slides.inSimpleWords: Acute angles are small, right angles are corners, obtuse are wide.

image.alt: Types of Angles — Lines and Angles

slides.title: Measuring Angles
slides.storyContext: Meera teaches Raj to use a protractor to measure the angle formed by the book pages.

points.label: Protractor
points.text: A protractor is a tool to measure angles. Place the center on the vertex and read the degree marking.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use a protractor to measure angles in degrees.

image.alt: Measuring Angles — Lines and Angles

slides.title: Finding Angles Around You
slides.storyContext: Raj finds angles in his room: corner of floor (90°), clock showing 3:00 (90°), open notebook (varies).

example.problem: What angle does a clock hand make at 3:00 and 6:00?
example.solution: At 3:00, the angle is 90°. At 6:00, the angle is 180°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Clock hands make different angles at different times.

image.alt: Finding Angles Around You — Lines and Angles

slides.title: Angle Hunt
slides.storyContext: Meera challenges Raj to find and classify 5 angles in his home.

points.label: Challenge
points.text: Find angles at home: door frame (90°), pencil box lid, scissors opening, window corners.

slides.inSimpleWords: Look around and name the angles you see.

image.alt: Angle Hunt — Lines and Angles

slides.title: Lines and Angles Review
slides.storyContext: Raj summarizes what he learned: lines never end, rays have one start, angles form between two rays.

points.label: Lines
points.text: Infinite straight paths with no endpoints.

points.label: Segments & Rays
points.text: Segments have two endpoints, rays have one.

points.label: Angles
points.text: Formed by two rays meeting at a vertex.

slides.inSimpleWords: Lines, segments, rays, and angles are the building blocks of geometry.

image.alt: Lines and Angles Review — Lines and Angles

subject: Mathematics
title: Meera's Magic Numbers
hook: Meera finds hidden patterns in numbers while organizing her school supplies.

slides.title: Numbers Everywhere
slides.storyContext: Meera counts her pencils: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. She notices every number is made of pairs.
slides.inSimpleWords: Numbers follow patterns we can discover.

image.alt: Numbers Everywhere — Number Play

slides.title: Even and Odd Numbers
slides.storyContext: Meera arranges pencils in pairs. Some pencils pair perfectly (even), one pencil is left alone (odd).

points.label: Even Numbers
points.text: Numbers divisible by 2 with no remainder: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12...

points.label: Odd Numbers
points.text: Numbers that leave remainder 1 when divided by 2: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11...

slides.inSimpleWords: Even numbers divide by 2 perfectly, odd numbers don't.

image.alt: Even and Odd Numbers — Number Play

slides.title: Finding Factors
slides.storyContext: Meera arranges 12 pencils in different rectangular groups: 2×6, 3×4, 1×12.

example.solution: Factors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12 (numbers that divide 12 with no remainder).

slides.inSimpleWords: Factors are numbers that divide another number evenly.

image.alt: Finding Factors — Number Play

slides.title: Multiples
slides.storyContext: Raj notices that if 3 is a factor, then 3, 6, 9, 12, 15... are multiples of 3.

points.label: Multiple
points.text: A multiple of a number is the result of multiplying it by any whole number.

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiples are what you get when you skip-count.

image.alt: Multiples — Number Play

slides.title: Multiples and Factors Together
slides.storyContext: Meera asks: if 5 is a factor of 20, then 20 is a multiple of 5.

example.problem: List multiples of 4. Then find which numbers have 4 as a factor.
example.solution: Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20... Numbers with 4 as factor: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20 (same list!).

slides.inSimpleWords: If X is a factor, then numbers it makes are multiples of X.

image.alt: Multiples and Factors Together — Number Play

slides.title: Prime and Composite
slides.storyContext: Meera groups numbers: some (like 2, 3, 5, 7) can only be divided by 1 and themselves (prime). Others (like 4, 6, 8, 9) have more factors (composite).

points.label: Prime
points.text: A number with exactly two factors: 1 and itself. Examples: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13.

points.label: Composite
points.text: A number with more than two factors. Examples: 4, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12.

slides.inSimpleWords: Prime numbers can't be divided except by 1 and themselves.

image.alt: Prime and Composite — Number Play

slides.title: Identifying Prime Numbers
slides.storyContext: Raj tries to divide 13 by 2, 3, 4... None work. 13 is prime!

example.solution: 15 = 3 × 5, so it has factors 1, 3, 5, 15. It is composite.

slides.inSimpleWords: Divide by small numbers; if nothing works except 1, it's prime.

image.alt: Identifying Prime Numbers — Number Play

slides.title: Number Detective
slides.storyContext: Meera challenges Raj: find all prime numbers between 1 and 20, then find all multiples of 3.
slides.inSimpleWords: Use division rules to identify number patterns.

image.alt: Number Detective — Number Play

slides.title: Number Play Review
slides.storyContext: Meera and Raj summarize: even/odd divide numbers, factors divide evenly, multiples come from skip-counting, primes are special.

points.label: Concepts
points.text: Even (÷2), Odd (÷2 with remainder), Factors (divide evenly), Multiples (skip-count).

points.label: Special Numbers
points.text: Prime (two factors), Composite (more than two factors).

slides.inSimpleWords: All numbers have patterns in how they divide and multiply.

image.alt: Number Play Review — Number Play
